rule: Before choosing a strategic plan, verify that no forcing tactic changes the position immediately.
At every move, scan forcing candidates for both sides before examining quieter moves.
Treat the opponent's last move as information: ask what it attacks, enables, prevents, and abandons.
Create a short candidate list before calculating deeply.

principle: Compare Moves, Do Not Defend Your First Idea
rule: Try to disprove each candidate and compare resulting positions instead of collecting reasons to like the first move.
Judge a move by the position it produces, not by how active or attractive the move looks.
When no tactic or urgent threat exists, improve the piece contributing least.
After every move, identify newly opened lines, newly weak squares, changed defenders, and altered tactical possibilities.

principle: Prefer Reversible Moves Before Irreversible Ones
rule: When choices are equally useful, delay commitments that permanently change pawns, exchanges, or king position.

principle: Use Principles to Narrow and Calculation to Decide
rule: Let principles produce candidates, then let concrete analysis select the move.
Analyze moves that sharply restrict replies before branching into quiet alternatives.

principle: Stop at Quiet Positions and Evaluate
rule: End a calculation branch only when forcing moves have subsided, then evaluate the stable position.
Continuously note pieces that are undefended or defended only once.
Before initiating exchanges on a contested square, count attackers, defenders, and the order in which they can participate.
Before making an expected recapture, look for an in-between check, attack, or stronger capture.
Look for a defender assigned to two jobs that cannot both survive a forcing sequence.
When a target is adequately protected, calculate whether its key defender can be exchanged, deflected, pinned, or distracted.
Force an enemy piece away from a duty or onto a vulnerable square.
Check whether a king without flight squares is vulnerable to rook or queen penetration.
Judge a combination against the opponent's strongest resource, not the reply you hope to see.
Influence the central squares with pawns and pieces so your army has room and the opponent has fewer active routes.
Bring knights and bishops into useful play before making repeated moves with one piece.
Develop knights early when their natural squares are clear, while delaying bishops until the pawn structure reveals their best diagonals.
Secure the king and activate a rook before investing tempi in offensive operations.
Do not expose the queen to repeated attacks unless it wins something concrete.
Complete development so no pieces remain between the rooks and the queen can coordinate or move safely.

principle: Do Not Hunt Pawns While Behind in Development
rule: Treat extra pawns as secondary when collecting them costs multiple tempi and leaves pieces inactive.

principle: Open the Center When Better Developed
rule: Use pawn breaks or exchanges to expose lines when more of your pieces are ready.
Choose early moves that keep several sound structures available until the opponent reveals commitments.

principle: Learn Opening Plans More Than Moves
rule: Memorize the purpose, pawn breaks, piece placements, and typical tactical risks behind an opening line.

principle: A Pawn Center Is Both Asset and Target
rule: Use a broad pawn center for space, but support it because the opponent will attack its base and advance points.

principle: Attack a Pawn Chain at Its Base
rule: Undermine the least mobile supporting pawn rather than pushing only against the chain's advanced point.

principle: Attack Where Your Pawn Chain Points
rule: Use the space and lines on the side toward which your central pawns advance.

principle: Counter a Flank Attack in the Center
rule: When the opponent spends time on a wing, seek a timely central break.
Exchange pieces, especially active enemy pieces, to reduce congestion in a space disadvantage.

principle: Do Not Close the Center Without a Plan
rule: Before advancing a pawn to lock the center, identify which wing and which pawn break will create play.
Use extra territory to place pieces on better squares rather than pushing more pawns automatically.
Place a piece on a square that enemy pawns can no longer challenge.

principle: Open Lines When Your Pieces Are Better
rule: Transform superior activity into concrete access by opening files and diagonals.
Delay a capture or pawn advance when releasing tension would improve the opponent more than you.
Treat every pawn move as a permanent change to squares, lines, and future structure.
Do not create isolated, backward, or weak-color squares unless you receive activity, space, or another concrete benefit.

principle: Passed Pawns Must Be Advanced With Support
rule: Use a passed pawn to gain space and distract pieces, but coordinate its advance with the rest of the army.
Place a suitable piece directly in front of an enemy passed pawn to stop it and attack around it.

principle: Create a Passed Pawn From a Majority
rule: Use a local pawn majority to exchange opposing pawns and leave one passer.

principle: An Isolated Queen Pawn Is Dynamic and Static
rule: Use the isolated d-pawn's space and open files actively before it becomes a fixed endgame weakness.

principle: A Backward Pawn Is Weak Only If It Can Be Attacked
rule: Evaluate a backward pawn by accessibility, fixing power, and available breaks, not by shape alone.

principle: Doubled Pawns Can Give Useful Lines
rule: Weigh doubled pawns against the files, central control, and bishop pair gained in the exchange.
Before pushing a structural break, place pieces where opened lines and resulting squares favor you.

principle: King Pawn Moves Create Lasting Holes
rule: Advance pawns around your king only for a concrete defensive or attacking purpose.
Route knights toward protected central squares that enemy pawns cannot attack.
Use pawn breaks, exchanges, or rerouting to give bishops meaningful scope.

principle: The Bishop Pair Prefers Open Positions
rule: Preserve two bishops when the center is likely to open and targets exist on both colors.

principle: Good and Bad Bishops Depend on Pawn Placement
rule: Judge a bishop by whether its own pawns obstruct it and whether it can attack useful targets.
Use rooks on files without friendly pawns to penetrate or pressure targets.
Add a second rook when one rook cannot safely penetrate or win the file alone.

principle: Coordinate the Queen With Minor Pieces
rule: Use the queen to amplify piece pressure rather than operating alone.

principle: Exchange the Opponent's Most Active Piece
rule: When under positional pressure, seek a favorable trade of the enemy piece doing the most work.

principle: Do Not Trade Your Best Piece Without Compensation
rule: Preserve the piece that creates your activity unless the exchange wins material, structure, safety, or a favorable ending.
Spend time correcting a piece with no useful future rather than pretending it will become relevant.

principle: Bring More Pieces Than the Defender
rule: Build local superiority around the target before sacrificing or opening lines.
Use pawn breaks, exchanges, or sacrifices to create files and diagonals leading to the enemy king.
When kings castle on opposite wings, prioritize direct pawn storms and forcing play over slow material gains.
Identify and remove the piece controlling entry squares, flight squares, or key blocks around the king.

principle: Fix a Weakness Before Attacking It
rule: Prevent a target from advancing, exchanging, or escaping before piling up pressure.
When one target is fully defended, open play on the opposite wing or create another permanent problem.

principle: Launch a Pawn Storm Only With Central Security
rule: Advance wing pawns when the center is closed, your king is elsewhere, or central counterplay is controlled.

principle: Demand Concrete Compensation for a Sacrifice
rule: Sacrifice material only for calculable gains such as mate, perpetual check, material recovery, lasting king exposure, or dominating activity.

principle: Keep Queens When the King Is the Main Target
rule: Avoid queen exchanges when your principal advantage is an attack and the enemy king remains vulnerable.
Choose improving moves that also create a real threat the opponent must answer.
Name the opponent's concrete threat and its required conditions before choosing a defense.

principle: Meet a Wing Attack in the Center
rule: Seek central counterplay when the opponent has committed time and pawns to one flank.
Exchange the enemy units most responsible for threats, especially queens or key minor pieces.

principle: Return Material to Neutralize the Initiative
rule: Give back extra material when it completes development, trades attackers, or removes king danger.
Give the king an escape square when back-rank or mating-net danger is concrete.
Prefer defensive moves that improve pieces, attack the opponent, or create escape options.
Do not move or exchange the pawns and pieces controlling one color around your king without checking enemy access.

principle: Simplify Pressure Into a Defensible Ending
rule: Offer exchanges when the resulting endgame removes attack and remains structurally viable.
Before executing your own plan, identify the opponent's best improvement and consider preventing it cheaply.
Defend a strategically important square with more pieces than immediately necessary when it anchors your position or future activity.
Use the king as a fighting piece once mating danger and queens are reduced.

principle: Put the Rook Behind a Passed Pawn
rule: Place a rook behind a passed pawn, whether it is yours or the opponent's, when the file is accessible.
In king-and-pawn endings, arrange kings so the opponent must yield the critical entry square.
Create a passer far from the main pawn mass to divert the enemy king.

principle: Create a Distant Passed Pawn Before Cashing It In
rule: Use the threat of promotion to gain king activity or win pawns rather than pushing automatically.

principle: Centralize Before Starting a Pawn Race
rule: Improve the king and pieces before committing pawns to a race when no immediate breakthrough is required.
Preserve pawn tempi and structure until the move creates a concrete gain.

principle: Trade Pieces, Not Pawns, When Ahead
rule: When materially ahead, exchange active pieces while preserving enough pawns to win.

principle: Choose Rook Activity Over Pawn Grabbing
rule: Prefer checks, king restriction, and penetration when taking a pawn would make the rook passive.
Count moves to promotion, checks, captures, and king entry rather than relying on visual intuition.
Before committing a move, scan the destination and resulting position for checks, captures, and one-move threats by the opponent.
Use more clock time when the position changes irreversibly or several serious candidates exist.
Record your thoughts, candidates, and evaluations before consulting computer analysis.
Tag errors as calculation, evaluation, knowledge, time management, emotional, or process failures.
Learn connected patterns containing pieces, pawn structure, plans, and tactical motifs rather than isolated facts.
Review patterns and opening ideas at increasing intervals before memory fully disappears.

principle: Play Slow Games to Train Calculation
rule: Use longer time controls regularly so candidate generation and verification become deliberate habits.
Convert slogans into prompts you can answer at the board.

principle: Practice at the Edge of Your Ability
rule: Choose tasks difficult enough to produce errors but clear enough to support focused correction.
Build routines that reduce ordinary errors before chasing rare spectacular ideas.
